summary: New Jersey's long-watched Bearfort Mountain fire tower, rebuilt as a 68-foot steel tower in 1934 after the prior wooden tower burned in 1932.

facts.design: 68-foot steel tower, McClintock-Marshall design, possibly supplied by Aermotor

staffing.as_of: NHLR observer reports describe an active, staffed tower

access.note: on the Newark watershed property in a heavily used recreation/hiking area; active NJ Forest Fire Service lookout, not open for public climbing

visit.trail_note: road up the mountain usable for most cars per a 1920s-era account; also reached by hiking trails

events.note: watcher stationed with telephone line and watch house added under Weeks Law agreement with City of Newark
prior wooden tower burned down after a stovepipe spark caught the roof; warden Charles Stalter on duty
registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, December 15, 1997

evidence.quote: An iron frame tower was built in 1909 by the Newark, NJ Watershed Department, and replaced with a 50' wooden tower which burned in 1932. A tree platform was used until the current 68' steel tower was built in 1934. It is a McClintock-Marshall design and may have been supplied by Aermotor under contract.

evidence.supports: cab condition noted in an observer report
evidence.quote: Inside of cab needs cleaning and re painting badly and general clean up... Alidade itself is broken and in bad condition.

The first thoroughly equipped and continuous forest fire lookout in the State was installed this season under this agreement (Weeks Law) and through the generous co-operation of the Board of Street and Water Commissioners of Newark.

A paradox was written into fire annuals last Friday when the old Bearfort Mountain fire tower burned to the ground. It was believed to have caught from sparks flying from a stove pipe into a rent in the tar paper roof of the look-out box. Charles Stalter, of Hewitt, fire warden on duty, had not reached his home before he was overtaken with word of the disaster.

evidence.supports: road access usable for most cars
evidence.quote: The road up the mountain from this point is steep but usable for most cars.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR says a wooden platform c.1880 and an iron-frame tower built 1909 preceded the 1932 fire; a 1923 newspaper excerpt on easternuslookouts instead describes a 40-foot frame tower 'built for the Forest Fire Service in 1916'; Wikipedia's footnote cites an even earlier Newark Watershed lookout from 1884. Left as an unresolved discrepancy rather than picked.

sources.title: List of New Jersey Forest Fire Service fire towers

notes_for_editor: Pre-1934 tower chronology is genuinely muddled across sources (1880s platform / 1909 iron tower / 1916 frame tower claims); worth noting as unresolved rather than picking a version. Exact April 1932 fire date not pinned down beyond 'last Friday' before an April 15, 1932 article.
